claims.claim: The sociological imagination is the ability to see how a person's private experience connects to larger social forces; C. Wright Mills introduced the concept in his 1959 book The Sociological Imagination.

OpenStax presents Mills' description of the sociological imagination as an awareness of the relationship between a person's behavior and experience and the wider culture that shaped that person's choices and perceptions — a way of seeing behavior in relationship to history and social structure.
Mills distinguished 'the personal troubles of milieu' from 'the public issues of social structure' and called that distinction an essential tool of the sociological imagination.

A personal trouble occurs within the character of an individual and within the range of that person's immediate relations with others and is felt as a private matter; a public issue transcends local environments and is a public matter often connected to the organization of institutions.

Mills' own unemployment example: when one person in a city is unemployed that is a personal trouble, but when millions are unemployed across a nation that is an issue whose solution cannot be found within the opportunities open to any one individual — 'the very structure of opportunities has collapsed.'

Mills argued that the sociological imagination lets people grasp the interplay of biography and history: neither the life of an individual nor the history of a society can be understood without understanding both.

The sociological imagination shifts explanation away from individual character toward the social conditions surrounding many similar lives; OpenStax notes that to a sociologist, personal decisions do not exist in a vacuum — cultural patterns and social forces put pressure on people's choices.
C. Wright Mills (1916-1962) was an American sociologist, long on the Columbia University faculty; The Sociological Imagination (1959) was a critical evaluation of the status of sociology.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Textbooks phrase the working definition of the sociological imagination differently (e.g., OpenStax's 'awareness of the relationship between a person's behavior and experience and the wider culture' vs. other texts' 'understanding the connection between personal troubles and public issues').
positions: OpenStax 3e frames it as an awareness/way of seeing behavior in relation to history and social structure.
The primary source (Mills 1959) emphasizes the troubles/issues distinction and biography-history interplay as its most fruitful tools.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches a Mills-attributed working definition that combines both: the ability to see how personal experience connects to larger social forces, with the troubles/issues distinction and the biography-history interplay as the concept's core tools. No single canonical wording exists; the lesson states its own working definition explicitly.

sourceRecords.title: The Sociological Imagination (1959), Chapter One: 'The Promise' — C. Wright Mills
sourceRecords.provider: Oxford University Press (author: C. Wright Mills)
sourceRecords.notes: Primary scholarly source. Canonical publisher product page registered; Chapter One ('The Promise') was read 2026-08-22 from a course-hosted PDF copy of the chapter (Middlebury College course site; the lending-restricted Internet Archive scan sociologicalimag0000cwri was not full-text searchable). Supports: the sociological imagination as a quality of mind enabling its possessor to understand the larger historical scene in terms of its meaning for the inner life and the external career of individuals; the distinction between 'the personal troubles of milieu' and 'the public issues of social structure'; troubles as occurring within the character of the individual and the range of immediate relations, issues as transcending local environments; the one-unemployed-person vs fifteen-million-unemployed example; 'neither the life of an individual nor the history of a society can be understood without understanding both.' Ideas summarized in original prose; no wording reproduced.
